items.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: of course Oscar and Ray and Ed Thigpen wiped us out

ctx.x: Oh, that’s great. That’s about as good as it gets for a musician. I want to ask you to elaborate on one thing here for us. You, I’ve heard you, through our conversation so far, again and again talk about the feel of music. And then you talked about having fun with the music and laughing and the grooves that you get into. Kind of give us your take on why those things are so essential to jazz. Not that orchestral music or chamber music doesn’t have a given energy. But talk to us from the jazz standpoint of why…

Well I just think it’s very important. In the classical thing the music is based more on the conductor, who, if it’s a conductor with charisma, with that energy, I mean these things in the orchestra usually come through, they have that pop. I mean in Chicago I used to go and listen to the Chicago Symphony. And they would be cooking. Cooking. I mean you know it was all I could do to sit still, because the energy or what the orchestra was about, generally was so great. And in jazz, I just feel it’s important. I…
It’s okay to get wiped out by people like that.
